document.title: Afghanistan: The War in Perspective (SNIE 37-89, Key Judgments only)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: November 1989 SNIE reckons that despite military withdrawal the Soviets will provide "massive aid" to their client regime, while Kabul will try to negotiate separate truces with "local resistance commanders." Originally published in CIA, At Cold War's End (1999).

key_claims: The Kabul regime is weak, unpopular and factionalized but will probably remain in power over the next 12 months.
The Mujahedin hold the initiative in the countryside but cannot prevent Soviet resupply or easily seize major garrisons.
The conflict is best understood as an insurgency in which political factors and Mujahedin disunity matter as much as military ones.
The Afghan Interim Government and major commanders will refuse direct negotiations unless Najibullah departs.
Pakistan will keep supporting the resistance whoever governs.
A unilateral US cutoff would favor the regime, while a unilateral Soviet cutoff would devastate it.
Even with aid cuts the conflict would likely continue indefinitely at lower intensity.
